name: Liquidity Stress Testing
title: Liquidity Stress Testing
answer: Liquidity stress testing measures whether a firm can keep meeting its payment obligations when funding conditions deteriorate. It covers cash inflows and outflows across business lines, off-balance-sheet commitments, and contingent claims such as undrawn credit lines or collateral calls. The exercise typically spans short-term horizons of a few days to several months, with severe but plausible scenarios that combine market shocks, rating downgrades, and operational disruptions. Its purpose is to identify potential funding gaps before they become unmanageable and to inform the size and composition of liquidity buffers.

sections.body: Liquidity stress testing measures whether a firm can keep meeting its payment obligations when funding conditions deteriorate. It covers cash inflows and outflows across business lines, off-balance-sheet commitments, and contingent claims such as undrawn credit lines or collateral calls. The exercise typically spans short-term horizons of a few days to several months, with severe but plausible scenarios that combine market shocks, rating downgrades, and operational disruptions. Its purpose is to identify potential funding gaps before they become unmanageable and to inform the size and composition of liquidity buffers.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on consolidated cash flow data from treasury systems, general ledgers, and loan or deposit platforms, joined with contractual maturity schedules and market data feeds. Scenario parameters, such as runoff rates or haircuts, are stored in controlled assumption libraries. Computation often takes place in treasury management systems, dedicated stress testing applications, or cloud-based analytics environments that can handle large volumes of position-level data. Outputs feed into dashboards and reports used by treasury, risk, and finance teams.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts define a baseline and a set of adverse scenarios, then project cash flows under each one. Contractual flows are adjusted using assumptions about customer behaviour, such as deposit withdrawal rates, prepayment speeds, and the drawdown of committed facilities. Market-based shocks are applied to collateral values, funding spreads, and foreign exchange rates. The results are compared against available liquidity sources, including central bank eligible assets and secured funding capacity, to calculate survival horizons and funding gaps.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Model risk management rules require that stress testing assumptions be documented, independently validated, and approved by a designated committee. Data lineage must be traceable from source systems to final reports, so that any number can be explained and reproduced. Access to change scenario parameters is restricted, and version control applies to models, assumptions, and results. Regulatory supervisors may review the methodology and outcomes, but this page describes common practice rather than giving legal or compliance advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Stress testing is moving toward more frequent and granular analysis, including intraday liquidity monitoring and scenario runs triggered by early warning indicators. Machine learning is being explored to estimate behavioural assumptions such as deposit stickiness and drawdown probabilities from historical data. Integration with asset and liability management and capital planning is becoming tighter, so that liquidity, interest rate, and solvency risks are assessed together. The direction is toward continuous, data-driven stress testing rather than periodic point-in-time exercises.
